## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dubbacajātaka* (Ja 116) is a canonical birth story belonging to the Jātaka collection in the Sutta Piṭaka [SuttaCentral]. The narrative opening relates that the Buddha told the story while staying at Jetavana, occasioned by an unruly or unadmonishable monk (*dubbacabhikkhu*), whose background circumstances are cross-referenced to the *Gijjhajātaka* in the ninth section (*Navanipāta*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. Addressing the unruly monk, the Buddha observes that he was equally obstinate in a former existence, meeting destruction by refusing to heed the instruction of the wise [Fausböll 1877].

In the story of the past, an acrobat skilled in the four-javelin dance becomes intoxicated and, despite warnings from his pupil, attempts to leap over five javelins, impaling himself fatally [Anandajoti 2010]. The verse underscores the need to observe proper limits, warning against excess and remarking that while skill and moderation may win a hundred, overreaching brings total ruin [Anandajoti 2010].

Neither SuttaCentral nor the computational analysis of DharmaNexus records any Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan collections [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral notes four translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
